title: Act II, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: After midnight Banquo, unable to sleep, tells Fleance of 'cursed thoughts' and gives Macbeth a diamond from the king for Lady Macbeth. Banquo mentions dreaming of the Witches; Macbeth claims he does not think of them and hints at future honor if Banquo will 'cleave to my consent'; Banquo agrees only if he keeps his allegiance clear. Alone, Macbeth sees a dagger in the air leading him to Duncan, wonders if it is 'a dagger of the mind', and goes when the bell rings: 'Hear it not, Duncan; for it is a knell.'

Next, craft. I notice the question he asks himself, which shows he cannot tell what is real. The strongest word is “dagger”: it is the weapon he is about to use, now appearing as a vision. Then, effect. What does the dagger vision show about Macbeth's mind? My answer: His mind is already guilty and disturbed; the dagger leads him toward Duncan's room, as if his imagination is pulling him into the crime.

When the text says “A dagger of the mind, a false creation, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain” (Act II, Scene I, Macbeth), it shows this directly.
